title: This is my mother, this is my father
title_target: Това е майка ми, това е баща ми
goal: Talk about family members and possession the Bulgarian way: short possessive words that stick to the back of the noun — "mother-my" instead of "my mother".
bekal: use the short possessives: **ми, ти, му, ѝ, ни, ви, им**
know when the noun takes the article and when it doesn't
ask and give ages with **на … години**
say someone is married using the right form

dialogs.title: Диалог — Family photos on the phone
dialogs.intro: Maria is looking at the photos on Ani's phone. Notice the pattern repeated throughout the dialogue: the noun comes first, and the possessive follows behind it.

notes: **The short possessives come AFTER the noun.** *Книгата ми* = my book. *Книгата ти* = your book. *Книгата му* = his book. The noun goes first and the possessive follows — the reverse of English "my book". Think "book-the my" and you've got it.

⚠️ **For ordinary things, the noun MUST take the article first.** Not *книга ми* but **книгата ми**. It makes sense: if it's yours, it's clear which one is meant. Think of it like this — *книгата ми* is literally "the book of mine".

⚠️ **But for the closest family members, the article is NOT used.** *Майка ми*, not *майката ми*. *Баща ми*, *брат ми*, *сестра ми*, *син ми*, *дъщеря ми*, *жена ми*, *мъж ми*. It's a small, closed group: parents, siblings, children and spouse. For more distant relatives the article comes back: *лелята ми* (my aunt), *братовчедът ми* (my cousin).

**The short possessives follow the same position rule as съм.** They can't be the first word in a sentence, and they stand right after the word they belong to. *Майка ми е учителка* — my mother is a teacher.

**Ѝ with an accent means "her".** Without the accent, *и* means "and". That one little stroke separates *книгата ѝ* (her book) from *книгата и*, which means nothing. People often skip it in handwriting and texts, but you should write it correctly.

**Age uses "at": на колко години си?** Literally "at how many years are you?" — and the answer is *На двайсет години съм.* The word *години* is never dropped, the way English can drop "years old". ⚠️ Don't say *Имам двайсет години*; that's French and Spanish word order, not Bulgarian.

**Женен for men, омъжена for women — and the roots are different.** *Женен* comes from *жена* (wife): "wived". *Омъжена* comes from *мъж* (husband): "husbanded". ⚠️ A woman who says *женена съм* immediately sounds like a foreign learner.

**Значи means "so, that means" and is used as a conversation linker.** Bulgarians use it as often as English speakers use "so" at the start of a sentence. Slipping it in makes your speech sound much more natural.

grammars.title: Short possessives — seven words that cover everything
body: Their form never changes with the thing owned; they only show **who the owner is**. Compare French or German, which demand double agreement.
after: Notice that these are exactly the same words as the "to me / to you" forms you've already used in *Приятно ми е* and *Дайте ми*. Bulgarian uses one set of little words for two jobs, and their position tells you which is meant.

grammars.title: Long forms — when you want emphasis
body: There are also long possessive forms. They behave like adjectives: they agree in gender and number with the thing owned, and carry their own definite article. They're used when the ownership is being stressed or contrasted.
after: *Това е моята книга, не твоята.* — This is **my** book, not yours. Outside contrasts like that, Bulgarians almost always use the short form. **When in doubt, use the short form** — it's shorter, more common, and needs no agreement at all.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Like English, Bulgarian has no separate words for older and younger siblings.** *Брат* just means brother. If age matters, an adjective is added: *по-голям брат* (older brother) and *по-малък брат* (younger brother) — literally "bigger" and "smaller".

Elsewhere Bulgarian is more detailed than English: there are different words for an uncle on your father's side (*чичо*) and on your mother's side (*вуйчо*). In everyday city speech *чичо* is often used for both, so don't worry.

Say it
Meaning
rows: На двайсет и пет години съм.
na DVAI-set ee pet go-DEE-nee săm

blocks.text: Questions about age, marital status and work are considered normal and friendly in Bulgaria, not nosy — quite different from much of Western Europe. If you get asked all of them in the first five minutes, the conversation is going well.

blocks.title: Имен ден — the name day, sometimes bigger than a birthday
items: Most Bulgarian names are tied to a saint, and that saint's day is the **имен ден** — name day — celebrated like a birthday. Everyone named Иван celebrates **Ивановден** on January 7; everyone named Георги celebrates **Гергьовден** on May 6.

The difference from a birthday: on a name day, **you don't need an invitation**. People can just drop by, and the person celebrating is expected to treat them. The greeting: *Честит имен ден!* (*ches-TEET EE-men den*).
If your Bulgarian colleague suddenly brings cake to the office for no obvious reason, this is most likely why.
